extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers interested in West African oral tradition and storytelling
extracted.subtask_description: Crafting or performing oral narratives in the West African griot (jeli/djali) tradition: memorized history, praise songs, and performative storytelling that blends music, poetry, social commentary and audience adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of oral communication and memorization
rubrics_metrics.description: Griots are masters of communicating stories and history orally; instead of writing history books, oral historians tell stories of the past that they have memorized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes the performer’s ability to hold large amounts of narrative in memory and deliver it reliably; the oral medium (rather than written text) is central to authenticity and function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of poetic and musical conventions to entertain
rubrics_metrics.description: Telling a story out loud allows the speaker to use poetic and musical conventions that entertain an audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performance should incorporate musical phrasing, poetic devices and rhythmic elements to engage listeners; these conventions help oral histories survive across generations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve and pass on cultural values through storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Through their storytelling, griots preserve and pass on the values of a tribe or people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narratives often carry moral guidance, social instruction and community memory; storytellers have responsibility to transmit cultural norms and genealogies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social role: advisor, mediator, and ability to address elites
rubrics_metrics.description: The griot is a repository of oral tradition and is often seen as a leader due to their position as an advisor to members of the royal family; they also act as mediators in disputes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A storyteller must be able to navigate social hierarchies, approach parties neutrally, and use speech strategically to mediate conflict or advise leaders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heteroglossia — structuring speech for multiple meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: Skilled griots structure their speech so that multiple meanings can be interpreted from the same message; this practice is referred to as heteroglossia, a sort of controlled ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft language that supports layered interpretation—surface praise, concealed critique, or double-entendre—allowing messages to resonate differently with varied audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to criticize and exert social influence
rubrics_metrics.description: With the privilege of being a neutral mediator, griots had the freedom and expectation to criticize and keep in line those with a higher social status; their professional authority allowed them to speak honestly in public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective storytellers can use verbal power to challenge or reinforce social norms; performance may include sanctioned criticism of elites as part of social regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embodied performance by women (griottes): vocal, gestural, and visual transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Women griots (griottes) demonstrate authority through embodied performance: soft voices turn into loud vocal projections and expressive gestures; their clothes also symbolize transformation (bright colors, jewelry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Female performance emphasizes embodiment—voice modulation, physicality, costuming and ritualized behavior—to enact characters, give moral instruction, and mark caste identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apprenticeship and hereditary transmission of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Griot traditions are passed on through hereditary apprenticeship systems in which children born into jeli families are raised from an early age in verbal art, music, and genealogy; they learn through observation, repetition, and guided participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training favors learning-by-doing rather than classroom drills: practice short repeated passages of real pieces, expand them over time, and learn adaptation techniques for audiences and contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrumental specialization and musicianship
rubrics_metrics.description: Griots are often skilled instrumentalists; instruments include the kora, khalam/xalam, ngoni, kontigi, goje, balafon and junjung. Instrumental specialization may be hereditary and gender based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proficiency on traditional instruments (and knowledge of their repertory) is expected; choices of instrument and playing style shape the performance and can be gendered in some communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation to audience and social context
rubrics_metrics.description: Oral transmission is not only memorization but also interpretation and adaptation: griots learn basic stories and musical structures while at the same time learning how to adapt performances to specific audiences and social contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performances should be responsive—modifying content, tone, and musical arrangement according to setting (weddings, courts, public commemorations, concert halls) and patronage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing tradition and modern innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinction between traditional and modern griots is fluid: 'traditional' often refers to older instruments and works, while 'modern' represents performances with new technologies and global influence; these elements are frequently combined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective contemporary practice may integrate amplification, electric instruments, recording technologies and global styles while maintaining inherited song traditions—innovation within continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative domains and ceremonial functions
rubrics_metrics.description: A village griot would relate stories of births, deaths, marriages, battles, hunts, affairs, and other life events; they are essential at events such as weddings where they sing and share family history and give moral guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Story content should be appropriate to the event: praise songs, genealogies, epic narration or moral instruction, with awareness of ritual obligations and expectations tied to specific ceremonies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtuosity as culmination of long study and the constraints of caste/patronage
rubrics_metrics.description: The virtuoso talents of the griots command universal admiration; this virtuosity is the culmination of long years of study under the tuition of a teacher (often a parent). Historically, griots formed an endogamous specialised group or 'caste' with associated social norms and patronage relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect long-term, lineage-based cultivation of skill and repertoire; social expectations (marriage within lineage, patron-client relationships) and historical constraints shape the practice and transmission of the art.
